title: The bottleneck of AI game dev is not coding. It’s testing.
author: Aikoioio
selftext:
Code can be “correct” in 1 minute. But making something feel right can take hours. You have to sit there, hands on the keyboard and mouse, eyes on the screen, with no distractions.  
  
That’s why 99% of game dev is frustration. The remaining 1% is the tiny moment when it suddenly feels alive, and you want to keep going.  
  
But strangely that difficulty makes me feel calm, because games are not built by code that works. They are built by people who take the time and notice when something feels wrong.

comments.author: RatbyteGames
comments.body:
I'm right in playtesting hell right now...

1) Playtest my game, write down ten bugs/tweaks/mods

2)do fixes, go to step 1

I'm up to the 50th iteration it feels like, them bugs still popping up.

replies.author: MDRAR
replies.body: Make sure you’re considering whether deeper architectural changes or adoption of engineering patterns might help close off whole categories of bugs instead of fixing what might feel like the same/very similar bug over and over.

replies.author: Aesthetic-Engine
replies.body: What engine are you using? If it's Godot you can pretty easily have Cursor/Codex/Claude test your game for you, create bug reports and fix them all in the same run

replies.author: baroldnoize
replies.body:
Could you build some kind of automated regression testing system? If you can wire up an AI to do those play tests then it gives it a feedback loop that might help it make changes without breaking old expected functionality.

It wouldn't be completely hands off, as you can't test for everything a human would pick up, but if it helps reduce the times when issues crop up and help AI complete its changes while validating it's not caused a regression issue that could really speed up your process and accuracy!

comments.author: blightor
comments.body:
Don't be in a hurry, this is actually why so many of the games turn out slop.  They have a handful of tests they outsource to a forum post, because AI doesn't do it for them very well (and eats mega tokens and just says what you want it to say).

If you are an easily bored person, you will fail here unless you put in the effort.  If your are just making another copy of an existing game, then you can probably just fall back on those classic games ideas and mechanisms - but what have you made?

comments.author: ClueHappy324
comments.body:
... and refactoring!

AI is insanely helpful along my indie game dev journey, but you really have to check and double-check all of its output. For example, I'm using AI to coauthor my design doc space (basically just translating my thoughts into a coherent format). It can produce *a lot* and *very quickly*, which is exciting, but you really have to pump the brakes, read all output yourself, and make hand-edits where necessary.

I'm an SWE by trade. While it's exciting to let AI take the wheel, the amount of refactoring I'm doing is insane. My workflow has converged on: Prompt -> Playtest -> Iterate with AI to get it right -> refactor. Once it has working code and a test suite (non-negotiable, all code is unit tested), it's amazing at refactoring without regression. If you don't do this frequently, smelly code just propagates.

replies.author: ParadisePrime
replies.body:
I don't think they're talking about real time generated games. I think they mean AI assied games.

AI can get you the code and foundation, but you have to actually go through and tune, iterate over and over and over again while having a strong vision of your game.

AI gets your vision into a playable state in 1-4 weeks and then you spend weeks to months tuning, going back and forth with it and then you get it polished. If you don't have a strong vision, this section will probably take very long.
